extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy, and scientific/scientific-method instruction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for analysing and judging chains of reasoning: when inferences are legitimate, how induction and deduction relate, how to identify and verify the 'marks' (attributes) that justify generalisations and their application to particular cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish identical versus distinct assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether one proposition merely repeats the very fact asserted in another (identical assertion) or whether the two propositions assert bona fide different facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If identity can be seen from the form/language, treat as repetition; if the propositions assert genuinely different facts, whether one proves the other cannot be decided from language alone and must be decided by induction (other considerations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step structure for applying generalisations
rubrics_metrics.description: Break reasoning into (1) ascertaining what attributes are marks of the target property and (2) deciding whether particular individuals possess those marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat all reasoning as if it takes this two-step form to enable application of tests for correct performance: first identify marks (general proposition), then identify marks in the individual (minor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify processes as Induction vs Deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify whether the process is establishing a general proposition from particulars (Induction) or interpreting/applying a general proposition to particulars (Deduction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider every inference about an unobserved case as consisting of an Induction followed by a Deduction; ensure the inductive foundation exists before treating the application as deductively secure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify inductive foundation of major premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Check that each general (major) premise used in reasoning is the expression of an induction founded upon observed instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Majors act as records of previous inductions; validity of conclusions depends on whether those inductions were correctly performed from sufficient instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace and evaluate trains of reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: When a minor premise is not directly observable and itself depends on inference, identify the chain (train) of syllogisms/inductions that support it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each added syllogism corresponds to another induction. Examine each link: what observations produced its major? Are the converging inductions consistent so the case falls within all required inductions?

rubrics_metrics.name: Require marks (attributes) to be inductively established
rubrics_metrics.description: Only treat an attribute as a mark (a satisfactory evidence) of some property if it has been shown, by induction, to be such a mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting 'A is a mark of B', cite or verify the induction(s) from observed instances that justify that claim; do not assume marks without inductive support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise marks-of-marks for indirect identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept that sometimes a case must be identified as possessing a mark only indirectly — by recognising marks of those marks (marks-of-marks) through successive inductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For cases not directly observable, check successive inductions that relate visible marks to deeper, less perceptible properties (e.g., a is a mark of b, b is a mark of c, therefore a can be used to infer c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat general propositions as formulae for inferring particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that general propositions/formulae are convenience records for inferring particulars from particulars and are not themselves the ultimate observed premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate reasoning by tracing back to the underlying individual observations (even if forgotten) that originally warranted the generalisation recorded in the formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure criteria/marks for applicability are explicitly determined
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine, once for all, the distinguishing marks by which cases are recognised as ones to which a given induction applies, so as to draw or avoid drawing a conclusion correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying a generalisation, check whether the target case exhibits the distinguishing marks specified by the formula; if not obvious, search for marks-of-marks that bring it within scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify combination of multiple chains converging on a conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: In more complex deductions, several separate chains (each yielding a mark) may unite to justify a final conclusion; ensure the combined marks jointly support the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect each chain's basis (its inductions/formulae) and confirm that their conjunction legitimately entails the desired property (example: optical/geometrical proofs combining three conditions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Check that inferred minors are themselves supported
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the minor premise is asserted by inference rather than immediate perception, require an independent induction or argument to establish that minor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept a minor simply because it would make the syllogism work; demand explicit justification (e.g., an argument showing 'Prussian government acts in manner X' before using it as a minor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess the correctness/sufficiency of the underlying inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: The legitimacy of any deductive application depends on whether the inductions on which the majors rest were correctly performed and applicable to the new case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sample size, representativeness, and convergence of independent inductions that underpin the generalisation; if an induction is weak, the derived deduction is unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer minimal and simple inductive bases for science
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructing a science, aim to base it on the fewest and simplest possible inductions (axioms/formulae) and use combinations of them to prove more complex truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields deductive power: complex cases are reduced to combinations of simple inductions. Judge a demonstration by how successfully it brings new cases under established simple inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use constructive ingenuity to bring unforeseen cases within formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: For cases not obviously matching available formulae, employ constructions or auxiliary comparisons (e.g., selecting pairs of angles in geometry) to bring them within the marks of known formulae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such contrivances are legitimate provided they legitimately establish the required marks; evaluate whether the auxiliary constructions truly yield the properties asserted and rest upon accepted formulae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on records and provenance for accepting past inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if original observations are forgotten or made by others, accept a generalisation if there is proof or record that those observations were once deemed sufficient for an induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand credible documentation or testimony that the induction was founded on observations considered adequate; treat unrecorded or undocumented inductive claims with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Deductive from Experimental character of a science
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether a science is Deductive (can derive properties of new cases by bringing them under old inductions via marks-of-marks) or Experimental (many new cases require fresh inductions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If propositions in the science can be connected via discovered marks-of-marks so that reasoning can proceed underground from visible marks to remote properties, it is deductive; otherwise it remains experimental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate attempts to transform experimental into deductive knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether new inductions legitimately bridge previously unconnected generalisations, enabling deductive derivations where before only separate experiments sufficed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge proposed connecting inductions (e.g., Dalton/Newton analogues) on their empirical scope and their ability to subsume formerly detached propositions into a unified deductive framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about disconnected generalisations and overgeneralisation
rubrics_metrics.description: When sciences produce many detached generalisations derived from disparate experiments, avoid inferring connections unless a bridging induction is established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that more observations often produce more disconnected truths; only accept inferred connections when supported by adequate new inductions rather than by wishful synthesis.
